body_markdown:
We’re fans of wagons around here. Estates, shooting brakes, longroofs, station sedans, depot hacks, carryalls—call them what you will. The extra utility gained by adding some cargo capacity behind the second row of seating is never a bad thing. In fact, many folks prefer the wagon variant of cars that also came as sedans and coupes. Olds Vista Cruiser, anyone? Chevy Nomad, anyone? Ahem, Volvo 1800ES?


Of course, some cars never came from the factory as wagons, but then famously one or three or a dozen were converted after the fact. Harold Radford’s Aston Martin DB5 and DB6 shooting brakes come to mind. Or Intermeccanica’s take on the 1966 Ford Mustang. Even Giovanni Bizzarrini’s Ferrari Breadvan, depending on how loosely we’re interpreting the genre. The point is that some cars you might not expect can be made into stunning wagons. Other cars, meanwhile, can be made into weird ones.


Take this 1987 Aston Martin Lagonda Series 3 shooting brake, for instance.[It sold on November 7](https://www.broadarrowauctions.com/vehicles/dg26_r0007/1987-aston-martin-lagonda-series-3-shooting-brake-by-roos-enginee) at Broad Arrow’s Zurich Auction for CHF 92,000 ($110,000).


Broad Arrow


Broad Arrow


Broad Arrow


In the mid-1970s, when Aston Martin’s new ownership group decided to aim upmarket at Bentley and Rolls, it did so with a William Towns design unlike anything else in the company’s portfolio. Long, low, and needle-sharp,[the Lagonda sedan](https://www.hagerty.co.uk/articles/a-lagonda-man-through-and-through/?_gl=1*kamxsg*_up*MQ..*_ga*MTczMDU3MzAyMC4xNzk0NDI3MDk5*_ga_C1Z3NGGXZT*czE3OTQ1MjQ0MTEkbzMkZzAkdDE3OTQ1MjQ0MTEkajYwJGwwJGgw) flew in the face of luxury-car convention. Its digitized spaceship controls did, too. Several well-publicized teething issues plagued it, such that three years passed between its 1976 introduction at the Earls Court Motor Show and first deliveries in 1979. But then there it was, fast as heck and priced to match, the perfect car for the petro kings and pop princes for whom old-money machines immediately felt too stuffy.


[The earliest Lagondas](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/aston-martins-outlandish-lagonda-turns-50/) relied on touch-sensitive switches and troublesome, hard-to-see LED gauges, which were eventually replaced with CRT readouts that came with their own issues, before bright, reliable vacuum fluorescent displays (VFD) were finally employed. But the exclusivity of the cars carried them forward, and over the ensuing decade they were refined incrementally through three series (somewhat confusingly called Series 2, 3, and 4, because of a previous, unrelated Lagonda sedan, the Series 1), with 645 built before production ended in 1990.


Broad Arrow


This Lagonda, s/n 13511, is one of 76 cars built during 1985–87 Series 3 production, generally considered to be[the most desirable variant](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/vellum-venom/vellum-venom-1983-aston-martin-lagonda/) for its use of VFD and Weber/Marelli fuel injection rather than carburetion. It was sold new in Switzerland and then changed hands in 1996. That owner commissioned Roos Engineering, a Swiss Aston specialist with a V8 Vantage shooting brake conversion already on its resume, to reinvent his Lagonda.


[In a 2024 interview](https://automobilrevue.ch/fahrberichte/ar13-007-009-drive-style-aston-martin-lagonda-interview) with Swiss magazine *Automobil Revue* , founder Beat Roos, an aircraft engineer by training, said of the four-year project, “I could envision building a vehicle that, in theory, shouldn’t even exist. I still remember the incredulous looks on my employees’ faces when I first presented them with the sketches.”


The initial work happened largely outside of regular business hours, Roos said. “Since our workshop was already pretty much at capacity with restorations and repairs, the design studies and feasibility studies had to take place on weekends in a somewhat quieter environment.”


Broad Arrow


Broad Arrow


Broad Arrow


Broad Arrow


During the conversion, Roos overhauled the car’s DOHC 5.3-liter V-8, with output now rated at more than 300 horsepower, and replaced the Chrysler TorqueFlite three-speed auto with a four-speed. The wagon retained its original wheelbase and overall length, with the cargo area built out from the rear of the sedan’s C-pillar, to include both a D- *and* an E-pillar. The car was fitted with $40K in custom windows and a slick hatch hinged about a foot into the roof, and the new and expanded interior was replaced with one finished in Connolly leather and Alcantara fabric.


Broad Arrow


Despite whatever disbelief his team might have held at the outset, the result was a wagon Roos believed even Towns would have approved of. “The crucial element was the sloping roofline, whose geometry absolutely had to be preserved,” he told *AR* . “After numerous sketches, drafts, and finally, with the help of paint, the goal was achieved, but it was a major challenge. The client immediately approved of the presented design and even said it might impress William Towns himself.”


It may be tempting to say there’s nothing else out there quite like this Lagonda shooting brake (which, let’s be honest, is a station wagon, because shooting brakes are two-doors…). But there is. At least two other Lagonda wagons exist, in fact: The Roos car came first, but it inspired Dutchman Harry Kielstra to[convert one in his garage](https://astonmartins.com/car/v8-lagonda-shooting-brake/) . And another[sold for $98,000](https://rmsothebys.com/auctions/mo19/lots/r0181-1987-aston-martin-lagonda-shooting-brake/) at RM Sotheby’s 2019 Monterey auction. That one, done by Swedish car and yacht designer Ted Mannerfelt, also took its inspiration from the Roos car. It’s an interesting exercise to compare[the rear-end treatment of all three](https://scontent-sea5-1.xx.fbcdn.net/v/t1.6435-9/52354555_810214722666209_4382895734794485760_n.jpg?stp=dst-jpg_tt6&cstp=mx2040x1708&ctp=s2040x1708&_nc_cat=105&_nc_map=urlgen_bucketless&ccb=1-7&_nc_sid=127cfc&_nc_ohc=CF3CMlkauGQQ7kNvwFKdxMr&_nc_oc=AdrUkY2-Gvpp-kQC5hb7JfxDuInzeuLszoEPWIu_tj9OG35fXBI0266fG5Z_jHSxZss&_nc_zt=23&_nc_ht=scontent-sea5-1.xx&_nc_gid=i-IDInt9Ziqd5L4-rpjNHg&_nc_ss=702a8&oh=00_AQTiz1Y9FsobGnKUdiUSiYaxgl6YManZcCcgXorN8nMrmQ&oe=6B1EC4CA) .


Broad Arrow


Our feature car was reportedly offered for sale in early 2016 by Swiss dealer Emil Frey Classics, for $425K. Later that spring, it was consigned to[Bonhams’ Aston Martin Works](https://cars.bonhams.com/auction/23592/lot/237/1986-aston-martin-lagonda-series-3-shooting-brake-chassis-no-13511/#photos) sale in the U.K., where it carried an estimate of £200K–£250K ($288K–$360K) but failed to sell.


Today, a Series 3 Lagonda sedan in #2 (excellent) condition is[a $94,000–$125,000 proposition](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/aston_martin/lagonda/1987/1987-aston_martin-lagonda-s3?id=aCn1I000000D5kNSAS&condition=excellent) . Typically, one car does not a market make, and it’s probably fair to say that two or even three cars don’t make it, either (as far as we know, the Dutch car has never been sold publicly). But when they’re literally the only cars in that market and they both fall far short of pre-sale expectations, perhaps there’s something to be gleaned from the reality of the hammer.


Ignoring inflation and the seven years between their sales, the fact that the RM Lagonda and the Broad Arrow Lagonda sold within 12 grand of one another seems instructive, particularly given that RM estimated its car to sell for $150,000–$200,000 and Broad Arrow gave this one an even more bullish estimate of CHF 250,000–CHF 350,000 ($299K–$419K). On the auction block in Zurich, however, this Lagonda’s rarity couldn’t quite trump its eccentricity. It would appear the market has spoken on Lagonda longroofs, however they’re called.


Broad Arrow
